task: Process journal: investigate an art movement or genre and critique one artwork from it, then show how you explored ideas practically and present a clear artistic intention for your final piece.
text:
Investigation: German Expressionism

Expressionism began in Germany around 1905 with the group Die Brücke in Dresden. Artists such as Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Erich Heckel rejected the realistic academic painting of the time because they felt it could not show what modern life felt like. Germany was industrialising fast and cities like Berlin were doubling in size, so their work is about inner emotion (anxiety, loneliness) rather than how things look. To do this they distorted figures, used clashing unnatural colour and borrowed the rough cut marks of woodcut printing, which they admired in medieval German prints.

Critique: Kirchner, Street, Berlin (1913)

The painting shows two fashionably dressed women on a crowded pavement surrounded by men in dark coats. The composition tilts steeply towards the viewer, so the street seems to slide out of the frame, and this made me feel unsteady, as if I was being pushed along by the crowd. The figures are stretched into sharp, mask-like shapes and painted in acid pink, blue and black with fast diagonal brushstrokes. None of the faces look at each other. I think Kirchner uses these choices to show that the city puts people physically close but emotionally separate. The pink is the most effective element because it should be a warm colour but here it looks sickly. A weakness, in my opinion, is that the men are almost identical, which makes the message a bit obvious, although it could be deliberate to show them as a faceless mass.

Developing my ideas

My theme is the pressure of the school corridor before exams. I tested three ways of making Kirchner's jagged line: charcoal, ink with a stick, and a small linocut. Charcoal smudged and looked too soft. The ink gave nervous lines but I could not repeat them. The linocut worked best because the tool forces angular cuts, and the uncut areas print as heavy black shapes like his coats. I then made three thumbnail compositions: a straight-on view, a view from above, and a tilted view with lockers leaning inwards. My classmates said the tilted one felt 'like the walls are closing', which is the effect I want.

Artistic intention

For my final piece I will make an A3 reduction linocut in yellow-green and black showing students in a tilted corridor, with elongated figures who do not look at each other. I intend the viewer to feel the crowded loneliness I found in Street, Berlin, but in a setting from my own life. I chose lino over paint because the cut marks carry the tension and because printing links to Die Brücke's woodcuts.

task: Process journal: investigate an art movement or genre and critique one artwork from it, then show how you explored ideas practically and present a clear artistic intention for your final piece.
text:
Pop Art started in the 1950s and 1960s in Britain and America. The artists used things from popular culture like adverts, comics and famous people. The main artists were Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein. They used bright colours and bold outlines, and Warhol used screen printing so he could make the same image many times. Pop Art was a reaction to abstract art, which people thought was too serious.

The artwork I chose is Marilyn Diptych by Andy Warhol from 1962. It has fifty pictures of Marilyn Monroe. The left side is in bright colours like orange, yellow and pink, and the right side is black and white and some of the faces are faded. I like the left side more because the colours stand out. I think the faded side might be about her death because she died that year. It is a good artwork because it is eye-catching and famous.

For my own work I took a photo of my trainers and drew it four times in my journal. I coloured each one with different marker colours. The blue and orange one looked the best because they are opposite colours. I also tried cutting a stencil but the paint went under it.

My final piece will be a Pop Art painting of my trainers repeated in a grid with bright colours, because trainers are something popular with teenagers today like soup cans were then.

task: Music, film-score unit: write an evaluation that appraises your final composition and reflects on how you have developed as an artist during the unit.
text:
My final piece is a 70-second score for the silent chase clip, written in GarageBand for strings, piano and percussion. My intention was to build tension steadily and then release it when the character escapes.

The strongest part of the composition is the opening. I used a low ostinato on the cellos, repeating the notes D and E flat, a semitone apart, because in my research on Bernard Herrmann I found that small intervals repeated create unease. When I played the clip to my class without telling them the story, seven out of nine people wrote 'nervous' or 'something is coming', so I can say this section achieved its purpose. The gradual accelerando from 90 to 130 beats per minute also worked, because it matches the cuts in the film getting quicker.

The middle section is less successful. I layered the ostinato, a piano melody and a snare pattern, and the texture became muddy; the melody, which was meant to be the character's theme, is hard to hear. My teacher's feedback said the same. Looking back, I added layers because I thought more instruments meant more excitement, when dropping the cellos out for two bars would have made the theme clearer and their return more powerful. The ending, where everything stops except one held high violin note, is effective, but the change to D major comes too suddenly. Two listeners said it sounded 'like a different piece'. A short rising passage to connect them would fix this. Overall the piece meets my intention for tension but only partly for release.

As a musician I have changed in three ways during this unit. First, I used to start with a melody and add chords; now I start with the mood and choose the element (rhythm, texture, register) that will create it. Second, I learned to use silence and thin textures, although the middle section shows I do not trust this yet. Third, my process improved: in week two I threw away a whole draft, and at the time it felt like failure, but exporting versions and comparing them taught me to listen as the audience, not the composer. I also became better at using feedback, since at the start I only asked friends if they 'liked it', which told me nothing.

Next I want to learn to write for real players, because the software strings cannot shape a note the way a person does, and my own piano skills limit what I can try out.

task: Music, film-score unit: write an evaluation that appraises your final composition and reflects on how you have developed as an artist during the unit.
text:
For my final piece I made music for the chase clip using GarageBand. I used strings, drums and piano. I think my composition went well overall and I am happy with it.

The start of my piece is quiet with low notes and then it gets louder and faster when the chase begins. I think this works because it fits what is happening in the video. I used a minor key because minor sounds sad and scary. The drums come in at 20 seconds, which makes it more exciting. One thing that did not go so well is the ending, because it just stops and I ran out of time to finish it properly. My teacher said that some parts were too loud compared to others. If I did it again I would fix the ending and change the volumes.

In this unit I learned a lot about film music and how composers use it to make feelings. I also learned how to use GarageBand better, like using loops and recording with the keyboard. At the start I did not know how to do this. I think I have improved as a musician because I can now make a whole piece by myself, and I managed my time better than in the last unit, although not perfectly.

task: Explain the health and fitness knowledge relevant to improving performance in a sport or activity of your choice, then design a six-week training plan with goals, explaining and justifying your choices.
text:
Knowledge and understanding

My activity is the 1500 m, which I run in 6 minutes 12 seconds. The event lasts long enough that most of the energy comes from the aerobic system, where the heart and lungs deliver oxygen to working muscles, so the key component of fitness is cardiovascular endurance. However, the final 200 m relies on the anaerobic system, which produces energy quickly without oxygen but creates lactate, causing the heavy, burning feeling in the legs. My race splits show my problem: my first three laps are 92, 98 and 104 seconds, and then I speed up again at the end. I slow down sharply in the middle, which suggests my aerobic base is weak and I am working above my lactate threshold too early, rather than lacking speed.

Training improves this through adaptation. Regular endurance work increases the heart's stroke volume and the capillaries around the muscle, so more oxygen arrives per beat. The principle of progressive overload says the load must increase gradually, and specificity says training must match the demands of the event. The FITT principle (frequency, intensity, time, type) is how overload is controlled.

Goals

My outcome goal is to run 1500 m in under 5:55 by the end of week six. My process goals are to keep every lap in a time trial within 4 seconds of the others, and to complete three sessions per week. These are measurable with a stopwatch and my training log, and realistic because a 17-second improvement is under 5 percent.

Plan

I will train three times a week (Monday, Wednesday, Saturday) with rest days between. Monday is a continuous run at 65-75 percent of maximum heart rate, starting at 20 minutes and adding 3 minutes each week; I chose this to build the aerobic base that my splits show I lack. Wednesday is interval training, 5 x 400 m at target race pace (94 seconds) with 90 seconds' rest, adding one repetition in weeks three and five; intervals are specific to race pace and raise my lactate threshold. Saturday is a 25-minute fartlek on grass, which mixes both systems and is softer on my shins.

Weeks one to five overload gradually and week six cuts volume by a third before the final time trial, so I am rested. I will time-trial in weeks three and six and record resting heart rate each Monday; if it rises by more than 5 beats I will replace the next session with rest. I considered adding strength training, but with only six weeks I judged that specific running would give the larger gain.

task: Explain the health and fitness knowledge relevant to improving performance in a sport or activity of your choice, then design a six-week training plan with goals, explaining and justifying your choices.
text:
My sport is basketball and I want to improve my fitness for it. In basketball you need lots of components of fitness. Cardiovascular endurance is needed because a game is four quarters and you run up and down the court the whole time. You also need agility to change direction quickly when you are defending, and power in your legs for jumping to get rebounds. Speed is important for fast breaks. I get tired in the third quarter and my coach takes me off, so I think my cardiovascular endurance is my weakness.

To improve fitness you need to use the FITT principle, which stands for frequency, intensity, time and type. You also need progressive overload, which means making training harder over time so your body keeps improving.

My goal is to improve my endurance so I can play a whole game without getting tired.

My plan is for six weeks. I will train three times a week. On Tuesdays I will go for a 20 minute run. On Thursdays I will do shuttle runs and skipping in the gym. On Sundays I will play a game with my friends at the park. Every two weeks I will add five minutes to the run. I will do a warm up before each session so I do not get injured. I will do the bleep test at the start and the end to see if I improved.

task: At the end of the team and net games unit, write a reflection that explains the strategies you used to enhance your interpersonal skills, and analyses and evaluates the effectiveness of your training plan and your own performance.
text:
Interpersonal skills

In our volleyball team of six I was the setter, which means I touch the ball on almost every rally, so communication was my responsibility. At first we lost points because two players went for the same ball or nobody did. The first strategy I used was to make us agree on three calls ('mine', 'out', and the name of the hitter I was setting to) and practise them in every warm-up, not only in games. By the third lesson the number of balls dropping between players went from about six per set to one or two, according to the tally our substitute kept. The second strategy was about encouragement. Ibrahim, our weakest server, stopped wanting to serve after two faults in a row. Instead of telling him to 'just get it in', I asked him what he found hard, and he said the toss. We spent ten minutes of two lunchtimes on only the toss. This worked better than general praise because it gave him something specific to control. One strategy that did not work was giving feedback during rallies; teammates said it was distracting, so I changed to speaking only between points. I learned that when I communicate matters as much as what I say.

Effectiveness of my plan

My plan aimed to raise my setting accuracy from 11 out of 20 into the target hoop to 16 out of 20 in five weeks, using wall sets three times a week and partner sets in lessons. I reached 15, so the goal was almost met. The wall drill was effective for hand shape and consistency, as my scores rose every week. However, the plan had a weakness I did not see when I wrote it: all my practice was from a perfect feed, standing still. In matches the pass is rarely perfect, and my accuracy when I had to move first was far lower. The plan was therefore effective for the test but less effective for the game.

My performance

In the final tournament my serving was reliable (17 of 19 in) and my decisions improved, for example setting to the back when the block followed our main hitter. My weakness was setting under pressure after a bad pass, where I often just pushed the ball over, wasting an attack. Overall I judge my performance as good in closed skills and only satisfactory in open play. Next unit I will design drills with unpredictable feeds and ask a partner to record sets from off-target passes separately, so that my data measures what really happens in a game.

task: At the end of the team and net games unit, write a reflection that explains the strategies you used to enhance your interpersonal skills, and analyses and evaluates the effectiveness of your training plan and your own performance.
text:
In this unit we played badminton doubles and I was partners with Chloe. To improve our interpersonal skills we tried to communicate more. At the start we kept hitting each other's rackets because we both went for the shuttle. We decided that one person would be at the front and one at the back, and we said 'yours' or 'mine'. This helped us a lot and we argued less. I also tried to be positive and say 'unlucky' when she missed a shot, so she would not get annoyed.

My plan was to improve my backhand clear by practising it for ten minutes every lesson and at badminton club on Thursdays. I think my plan was quite effective because my backhand got better. At the start I could only hit it to the middle of the court and now it sometimes reaches the back. I missed two club sessions because of a school trip so I did not do all of the plan.

In the final matches we won three games and lost two. My serve was good and I did not make many mistakes with it. My backhand was still my weakest shot and the other team hit it to that side a lot. I also got tired in the last game. Next time I would practise more and work on my fitness as well.

task: Design folio, inquiring and developing: justify the need for a solution for a client, outline your research plan, analyse existing products and write a design brief; then write a design specification, present a range of ideas and justify your chosen design with planning details.
text:
The problem and my client

My client is my grandfather, who is 78 and takes five different tablets at three times of day. Twice this month he took his evening tablets in the morning. In an interview he told me that his current pill box has lids that are 'too stiff for my thumbs' because of arthritis, and that the printed days have rubbed off. A solution is needed because wrong doses of blood-pressure medication are dangerous, and because he wants to manage his medicine independently.

Research plan

My primary research was the interview, a timed observation of him filling and opening his box, and measurements of his hand span and the tablets. My secondary research was arthritis design guidelines. I prioritised the observation, since it shows what he actually does rather than what he says.

Analysis of existing products

The weekly strip box (about 4 euros) is cheap and portable but has small snap lids, which he could not open in two of five attempts. The push-button organiser opens easily, but the lids spring up and tablets jumped out. The electronic dispenser with an alarm (about 60 euros) solves the timing problem but he found the buttons confusing and it needs charging. I concluded that easy opening and clear labelling matter more to him than technology.

Design brief

I will design and make a weekly pill organiser for my grandfather that he can open with limited grip strength, that shows clearly which dose is next, and that stays on the kitchen counter where he eats breakfast.

Specification

The product must: have 21 compartments (7 days x 3 times), each at least 30 x 25 x 20 mm to hold his largest dose; open with the side of the hand, without pinching; have labels at least 10 mm high with strong contrast, engraved so they cannot rub off; be stable on a worktop; cost under 15 euros in materials; and be wipeable.

Ideas

Idea 1 is a tray with sliding lids; Idea 2 is a rotating wheel with one opening; Idea 3 is seven removable day-blocks with hinged flip lids and a large tab; Idea 4 is a wall chart with hanging pouches. I tested card models of each with him.

Chosen design

I chose Idea 3. The flip lid with a 25 mm tab met the opening requirement in all five trials, whereas the sliding lids jammed. The wheel was his second choice but hides the other doses, failing the 'shows what is next' point. I will make it from 3 mm laser-cut plywood with acrylic lids; my drawings give dimensions for each part, the finger joints and the engraving layout.

task: Design folio, inquiring and developing: justify the need for a solution for a client, outline your research plan, analyse existing products and write a design brief; then write a design specification, present a range of ideas and justify your chosen design with planning details.
text:
My client is my older sister. She watches videos on her phone while she is cooking and doing her make-up, and she leans it against a cup and it always falls over. So she needs a phone stand. This is a problem for a lot of people because everyone uses their phone to watch things now.

For my research I asked my sister what she wanted and I looked on the internet at phone stands that already exist. I looked at two products. The first one is a plastic folding stand from Amazon. It is cheap and small but it looks boring and it only has one angle. The second one is a metal stand that can change angle. It is stronger and looks better but it costs more.

Design brief: I am going to design a phone stand for my sister that holds her phone so it does not fall.

Specification: It must hold her phone. It should be a nice colour (she likes green). It must not be too big. It should be cheap to make. It should be strong.

I drew three ideas. The first is a triangle shape made from wood. The second is a stand shaped like a cat where the tail holds the phone. The third is made from bent acrylic. I chose the acrylic one because my sister liked it the most and it looks modern. I will make it in the workshop using the line bender.

task: Design folio, creating and evaluating: present your plan for making the product, describe how you made it and justify any changes to the design; then explain how you tested it, evaluate it against your design specification, suggest improvements and explain its impact on your client.
text:
Plan for making

My product is a plywood laptop stand for my mother, who works from home and has neck pain from looking down at her screen. My plan had nine steps, each with the tool, time and a quality check: 1) print the templates at full size and check the 240 mm width against the laptop; 2) mark out on 9 mm birch plywood, with the grain along the legs for strength; 3) cut the two sides with the scroll saw, 2 mm outside the line; 4) cut three cross-slats; 5) sand to the line and check both sides are identical by clamping them together; 6) cut the 9 mm slots; 7) dry-fit without glue; 8) glue and clamp overnight; 9) sand from 120 to 240 grit and apply two coats of water-based varnish.

Making and changes

I followed the plan up to step 6. Cutting the slots, the scroll saw wandered and my first slot was 10.5 mm, so the slat was loose. For the remaining slots I drilled a 9 mm hole at the end of each and cut to it with the tenon saw, which gave a tight fit. I made two changes to the design. First, at the dry-fit the laptop slid forward, so I added a 12 mm lip at the front; without it the product would not function. Second, I reduced the slats from three to two wider ones, because three blocked the laptop's air vents, which I had not considered at the design stage.

Testing

I tested each point of the specification. For screen height I measured my mother's seated eye level (118 cm) and the top of the screen on the stand (114 cm, against 96 cm before). For strength I loaded it with 6 kg of books for 24 hours, three times the laptop's weight. My mother then used it for one working week and completed a short questionnaire.

Evaluation

The stand met five of the six specification points. Height, stability, strength and cost (7.40 euros against a 10 euro limit) were met with measured evidence. It did not meet 'can be stored flat', because I glued the joints after the loose slot made me doubt a push-fit.

Improvements

I would cut the parts on the laser cutter so the slots are accurate enough to fit without glue, which would restore flat storage, and add cork pads so it does not slide on a glass desk.

Impact

My mother reported less neck stiffness by Thursday and has kept using it, although she had to buy a separate keyboard, a cost that my design created and I had not predicted.

task: Design folio, creating and evaluating: present your plan for making the product, describe how you made it and justify any changes to the design; then explain how you tested it, evaluate it against your design specification, suggest improvements and explain its impact on your client.
text:
My product is a tote bag for my friend Maya to carry her books. My plan was: 1. Cut out the fabric. 2. Pin the pieces together. 3. Sew the sides and the bottom. 4. Make the straps and sew them on. 5. Add the pocket. 6. Iron it. I used the sewing machine, scissors, pins and an iron.

I made the bag over four lessons. First I cut two rectangles from the blue canvas using the paper pattern. Then I pinned them and sewed around three sides with a straight stitch. The straps were hard because the fabric was thick and the needle broke once, so the teacher helped me change it. I changed my design because I did not have time to do the inside pocket, so I left it out. I also made the straps a bit shorter than in my drawing.

To test it I put my school books in it and carried it around, and it did not break. I also asked Maya and two other people what they thought and they said it looked nice and they liked the colour.

I think my bag is successful because it works and Maya likes it. It matches most of my specification. If I made it again I would add the pocket and make the sewing neater because some lines are not straight. Maya can use it instead of plastic bags, which is better for the environment.

task: Write a condensed personal project report covering planning (learning goal and personal interest, product and success criteria, plan), applying skills (how ATL skills helped you achieve the goal and product) and reflecting (impact of the project on you and evaluation of the product against the success criteria).
text:
Planning

My learning goal was to learn how to service and repair bicycles well enough to safely restore an unused one. This comes from a personal interest: I cycle to school every day, but when my chain snapped last year I paid 35 euros for a repair I did not understand, and I disliked depending on someone else for something I use daily. My product was therefore one fully restored bicycle, donated to the school's lending scheme, plus a ten-page illustrated repair guide for students.

I wrote success criteria with the shed supervisor, Mr Okafor, so they would be specific and testable: the bike passes the 20-point safety checklist used by a local bike shop; the brakes stop it within 4 metres from 15 km/h; parts cost under 40 euros; the guide covers five common repairs; and three out of four year 7 students can fix a puncture using only the guide. My plan divided September to January into four phases (learn, strip and diagnose, repair, write and test the guide) with a deadline for each and a weekly log.

Applying skills

Research skills were the most important for my learning goal. I compared three sources for each repair (a mechanic's handbook, a video channel and Mr Okafor's advice) because early on a video told me to oil the brake rims, which the handbook showed is dangerous. After that I recorded where sources disagreed and tested the instruction myself. Self-management skills helped when the rear wheel bearings turned out to be rusted solid: I had allowed one week and it took three. I re-ordered my plan, writing the guide's first chapters while I waited for parts. For the product, communication skills mattered: my first draft used words like 'derailleur' without explanation, and a year 7 tester got stuck on page one. I rewrote it with labelled photographs and one action per step.

Reflecting

The project changed how I learn. I used to give up on practical problems quickly and look for someone to ask; now I expect the first attempt to fail and treat it as information. Evaluating the product, the bike passed 19 of 20 checklist points (the rear reflector was missing), stopped in 3.6 metres and cost 31 euros, so those criteria were met or nearly met. The guide covers five repairs, but only two of four students fixed the puncture unaided, so that criterion was not met; both who failed could not get the tyre back on, which my photographs do not show clearly. Overall the bike is a success and the guide only partly. With more time I would film that step and add a QR code to the page.

My learning goal was to learn how to cook traditional Lebanese food, and my product was a recipe book with ten recipes from my grandmother. I chose this because my family is from Lebanon and I love the food, but I only knew how to make basic things like pasta. I also wanted to keep my grandmother's recipes because she never writes them down.

My success criteria were that the book has ten recipes, has photos of every dish, is easy to follow and looks professional. My plan was to cook one recipe every weekend from October to December and then design the book in January.

The ATL skills I used were research skills, self-management skills and communication skills. I used research skills when I interviewed my grandmother and looked up recipes online. I used self-management skills to organise my time, although I got behind in December because of exams and had to cook three dishes in one weekend. I used communication skills when I wrote the recipes and when I talked to my supervisor.

This project had a big impact on me. I learned to cook lots of dishes and I became closer to my grandmother. I think my product is good. It has ten recipes and photos of each one, so it meets those criteria. My family said it was easy to follow and looks nice. If I did it again I would start earlier and add more recipes.

task: Paper 2: Compare how two works you have studied present characters who struggle against the expectations of their society.
text:
Both Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House (1879) and Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale (1985) place a woman inside a household that defines her by her usefulness to a man. Yet the two works imagine struggle very differently. Ibsen's Nora moves from unconscious performance to an open, spoken break with her society, whereas Atwood's Offred resists inwardly, through memory and language, in a regime where open defiance means death. I will argue that the form of each work, a realist stage play and a first-person retrospective narrative, shapes what kind of struggle is possible and how far we can trust its success.

In A Doll's House, society's expectations first appear as affection. Torvald's pet names, his 'skylark' and 'squirrel', reduce Nora to something small, decorative and owned, and in Act One she answers to them eagerly. Because this is drama, we have no access to her thoughts; we see only behaviour, and so the audience, like Torvald, initially takes the performance for the person. Ibsen undermines this through props and action. The macaroons Nora hides are a trivial disobedience, but they establish that she already lives a double life, and the forged signature reveals that the 'doll' has acted with more courage than her husband. Her struggle is at first not against expectation but within it: she breaks the law in order to be a good wife.

Atwood, by contrast, gives us almost nothing except thought. Offred's outward conformity is total: she wears the red habit, walks in pairs, speaks in prescribed greetings. Her resistance is located in the narration itself. She plays with words and savours the Latin joke scratched in her cupboard, because in Gilead, where women are forbidden to read, private language is the one territory the state cannot patrol. The fragmented structure, which slides between the Red Centre, her lost daughter and the present, enacts a refusal to let the regime fix her identity as a Handmaid. Where Ibsen shows a woman who does not yet know she is oppressed, Atwood shows one who knows precisely and can do very little.

The turning points sharpen this contrast. In the tarantella, Nora dances wildly while Torvald corrects her; the stage image makes visible both her desperation and his control. After his selfish reaction to Krogstad's letter she changes out of her costume, sits him down and, for the first time, they talk seriously, in plain, almost legal language that signals she has stopped performing. Offred has no equivalent scene. Her rebellions, the Scrabble games and the affair with Nick, are ambiguous, since each is partly arranged by those who hold power over her.

Finally, both endings leave the struggle unresolved. The door Nora shuts shocked contemporary audiences because the act is public and chosen, although Ibsen does not pretend that a woman without money or legal rights walks out into freedom. Offred steps into a van with no agency at all, and the Historical Notes then show male academics joking about her testimony, so that even her narrative is taken over by others. Ibsen's ending is the more hopeful, Atwood's the more sceptical about whether an individual voice can change a society.

In conclusion, both writers present the struggle against expectation as beginning in the self before it can become action. Ibsen, writing for the stage, makes that struggle visible and decisive; Atwood makes it private, compromised and uncertain. Together they suggest that resistance depends less on a character's courage than on how much room her society leaves her to speak.

task: Paper 2: Compare how two works you have studied present characters who struggle against the expectations of their society.
text:
A Doll's House by Henrik Ibsen and The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood both show women who struggle against what society expects of them. In this essay I will compare how Nora and Offred do this.

In A Doll's House, Nora is expected to be a perfect wife and mother. Her husband Torvald calls her names like 'skylark' and 'squirrel', which shows that he treats her like a pet or a child. At the start Nora accepts this, but she has a secret, which is that she borrowed money to save his life. At the end of the play she realises that Torvald does not really love her and she leaves him and her children. This was very shocking at the time because women did not do this.

Similarly, in The Handmaid's Tale, Offred lives in Gilead where women have no rights and Handmaids have to have babies for the Commanders. Offred struggles against this by remembering her old life and by having a relationship with Nick. Atwood uses first person narration so we know what Offred is thinking. The colour red is a symbol of the Handmaids.

However, the two characters are different because Nora leaves at the end but Offred cannot leave so easily and we do not know what happens to her. Nora's struggle is more successful.

In conclusion, both writers show that women struggle against society's expectations, but in different ways. Both works are still relevant today.

task: Individual oral: examine the ways in which the global issue of your choice is presented through the content and form of one literary extract and one non-literary text you have studied.
text:
The global issue I will explore is how those in power use language and images to persuade ordinary people to take part in war, and how artists can expose that persuasion. My literary extract is Wilfred Owen's poem 'Dulce et Decorum Est', written in 1917. My non-literary text is the 1915 recruitment poster 'Daddy, what did YOU do in the Great War?' by Savile Lumley, one of the posters issued by the Parliamentary Recruiting Committee. I will argue that the poster manufactures shame in order to recruit, while Owen uses the physical reality of the front to accuse exactly that kind of manufacture.

I will begin with the poster. Its setting is a comfortable post-war living room: an armchair, patterned curtains, a girl on her father's knee with a history book, a boy playing with toy soldiers on the floor. The war is therefore presented as already won and already safe, a subject for books and toys; no injury appears anywhere in the frame. The persuasion works through the caption. The question is put in a child's voice, which makes it impossible to answer with anger, and the capitalised 'YOU' singles out the individual viewer. The father's gaze is the key visual choice: he looks out at us, away from his daughter, with a troubled expression, so the viewer is invited to imagine his own future embarrassment. Across the Committee's posters this is a repeated strategy; others ask women whether their 'best boy' is in khaki. The body of work consistently turns a political decision into a private test of masculinity and family honour, and it never shows what enlisting leads to.

Owen's poem supplies what the poster leaves out. From the first line the soldiers are 'bent double, like old beggars under sacks', a simile that removes youth and heroism at a stroke; these are the men the toy soldiers stand for. The rhythm drags with heavy monosyllables until the gas attack breaks it open: 'Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!' The capitals and exclamations echo, ironically, the shouting typography of recruitment posters, but here they announce death. Owen then narrows to one man 'drowning' under 'a green sea', and the present participles 'guttering, choking, drowning' keep the death continuing, as it does in the speaker's dreams. Where the poster's father is troubled by a question, Owen's speaker is haunted by a face.

The final stanza turns directly on the persuaders. The shift to 'you', in 'If you could hear', mirrors the poster's 'YOU' but reverses its direction: the reader is not asked what he did, but whether he could bear to watch. The address to 'my friend' is bitterly ironic. Owen ends by naming the slogan itself, 'the old Lie', and by quoting Horace in Latin, the language of the schools that taught boys that dying for one's country was sweet. Significantly, the children who are 'ardent for some desperate glory' are the same audience as the boy on the poster's carpet.

Placing the texts together shows two sides of the issue. Both rely on direct address, on children, and on the viewer's imagination of a future moment. The poster uses these to hide consequences; Owen uses them to force consequences into view. However, Owen's poem reached few readers before 1920, while the posters were printed in their millions, which suggests that exposing persuasion is slower and weaker than persuasion itself. This matters today, when recruitment advertising and online propaganda still sell conflict to the young as adventure and duty, and it is why I think the issue remains global and urgent.

task: Your school is considering banning mobile phones during the school day. Write a text for the school community in which you give your opinion and suggest what the school should do. Choose the most appropriate text type: article, diary entry or set of instructions.
text:
Lock Them Away? Why a Phone Ban Would Teach Us Nothing

By Lukas Brandt, Year 12

Last week the school council announced that it is considering a complete ban on mobile phones during the school day. Walk through the canteen at lunchtime and you will understand why: rows of students, heads down, thumbs moving, hardly a conversation in sight. I admit that the picture is not a pretty one. Nevertheless, I am convinced that a total ban is the wrong answer to a real problem.

Let us start with what the supporters of the ban get right. Phones distract. A teacher of mine told me that she can see the exact moment when a class 'disappears' into their pockets, and nobody who has tried to revise with notifications switched on could seriously disagree.

However, banning phones does not make the distraction go away; it merely postpones it until four o'clock. Sooner or later all of us will work in offices, lecture halls or workshops where nobody will take our phones away. If school is supposed to prepare us for that life, then it has to give us the chance to practise self-control, and to fail at it occasionally, while the consequences are still small.

There are practical objections too. Many of us use our phones to check the timetable, to photograph the board, or to translate a word in a language lesson. Some students need to be reachable by parents who work shifts. A ban that ignores these needs would be broken within a week, and a rule that everybody breaks is worse than no rule at all.

So what should the school do instead? I would suggest three things. Firstly, phones should stay in bags during lessons unless the teacher asks for them. Secondly, the canteen could become a phone-free zone, so that at least one place in the building belongs to conversation. Thirdly, and most importantly, students should be involved in writing the rules. We are far more likely to respect an agreement that we helped to create than a ban that was handed down to us.

The council will vote next month. Before it does, I would ask its members to remember that the aim of a school is not silence in the corridors but young people who can manage their own lives. If you agree, or if you think I am completely wrong, come to the open meeting on Thursday in the library and say so. Just remember to put your phone on silent.

task: Your school is considering banning mobile phones during the school day. Write a text for the school community in which you give your opinion and suggest what the school should do. Choose the most appropriate text type: article, diary entry or set of instructions.
text:
Should Phones Be Banned in Our School?

Hello everyone! Today I want to write about the idea of banning mobile phones in our school. Many students are talking about this topic and I want to give my opinion.

In my opinion, banning phones is not a good idea. First, phones are very useful for learning. For example we can search informations on the internet when the teacher ask a question, and we can use the calculator or the dictionary. Second, phones are important for the security. If something happen, students can call their parents quickly. My mother always want to know where I am after school.

On the other hand, I understand that phones have also disadvantages. Some students are playing games in the lessons and they don't listen the teacher. Also there is the problem of cyberbullying, which is very serious.

But I think that the solution is not to ban all the phones. The school should make rules. For example, students can use phones only in the break and in the lunch time, and in the lesson the phone must be in the bag. If a student don't respect the rule, the teacher can take the phone until the end of the day.

To conclude, phones have advantages and disadvantages but I think a ban is too much. What do you think? Tell me your opinion!
